children: 1990年一个炎热的八月天，我第一次走进了斯大林统治下俄罗斯的内在世界。那正是“重建”（perestroika）的转折点，米哈伊尔·戈尔巴乔夫的自由化改革开始瓦解苏联秩序。对于历史学家来说，“重建”标志着一场档案革命的开始：共产党档案的大规模解密持续了20世纪90年代的大部分时间，促使人们对苏联的过去产生新的解读。我刚刚在莫斯科的图书馆里待了几个星期，为一个关于斯大林时期俄罗斯农民命运的研究项目收集资料。我的停留即将结束——再过两天我就要飞回纽约。俄罗斯朋友向我保证，早晨洗一次蒸汽浴就能抵御一天的酷热。洗完澡后，我走在市中心的街道上，隐约感到有些精力充沛。一座建筑上的招牌吸引了我的注意：“人民档案馆”。片刻犹豫后，我走了进去。

I first entered the inner world of Stalin’s Russia on a hot August day in 1990. This was during the turning point of perestroika, when Mikhail Gorbachev’s liberal reforms began to unravel the Soviet order. For historians, perestroika marked the beginning of an archival revolution: a massive declassification of Communist party records would continue through much of the 1990s, prompting new interpretations of the Soviet past. I had just spent several weeks in Moscow’s libraries collecting material for a research project on the fate of Russia’s peasants under Stalin. My stay was coming to an end—in a couple of days I would fly back to New York. After the morning steam bath my Russian friends had assured me would counteract the heat of the day, I walked through the streets of the city center in a vaguely energetic mood. A sign on a building caught my eye: People’s Archive. After a moment’s hesitation, I walked in.

起初我怀疑自己是不是走错了：我发现自己置身于一家简陋的小店，里面塞满了廉价的晶体管收音机和流行音乐磁带。但当我询问档案馆时，店员把我指引向一个面向院子的后屋。和大多数档案馆一样，那里阴暗凉爽；带铁栅栏的小窗户提供着微弱的照明。一排排金属架上摆着成列的大灰盒子。临时布置的阅览室和破旧的家具表明，让这个档案馆维持开放的是热情而非慷慨的资助。馆长当时不在；他的年轻助手们兴奋地告诉我，他们致力于收集和保存普通公民的声音，他们相信这些声音可以挑战压抑的苏联国家及其对个人和集体记忆的控制。

At first I wondered whether I’d made a mistake: I found myself in a seedy shop crammed with cheap transistor radios and pop music tapes. But when I inquired about the archive a shopkeeper directed me to a back room facing a courtyard. Like most archives, it was dark and cool; small barred windows provided the feeblest illumination. Ranks of metal shelves held rows of large gray boxes. The improvised reading room and its battered furniture signaled that enthusiasm rather than generous funding kept this archive open. It turned out that the director was away; his young assistants excitedly told me about their commitment to collecting and preserving the voices of ordinary citizens, which they believed could challenge the oppressive Soviet state and its sway over personal and collective memory.

很快我们的谈话就触及了斯大林的统治。当我谈到我的研究时，一位档案管理员从架子上取出了一个装满泛黄、蒙尘笔记本的盒子。我翻开最上面的笔记本，读到了如下标题：“‘团九大’旅工作日记及旅长、学生斯捷潘·菲利波维奇·波德卢布内每日笔记”。我读了下去，很快就被这个年轻人的故事吸引了：由于父亲是“阶级敌人”，他遭到了苏联政权的迫害。当波德卢布内逃离村庄到达莫斯科后，他设法隐瞒了自己那段被视为耻辱的过去，冒充模范工人和共产主义者。日记揭示了一种充满紧张和危险的双重生活；但最引人注目的是，它记录了这个男人重塑自我的尝试——他似乎渴望成为他所扮演的那个人。

Soon enough our conversation touched on Stalin’s rule. When I talked about my research, one of the archivists pulled from the shelves a box filled with yellowed, dusty notebooks. I opened the notebook lying on top and read the following title: “Work Diary of the ‘9thKomsomol-Congress’ Brigade and Daily Notes of the Brigadier and Student Stepan Filipovich Podlubny.” I read on and was soon absorbed by the story of a young man persecuted by the Soviet regime because his father was a “class enemy.” When Podlubny escaped his village and reached Moscow, he managed to conceal his shameful past and passed himself off as a model worker and Communist. The diary revealed a double life fraught with tension and danger; but most remarkably it documented this man’s attempts to remake himself—he seemed to yearn to become the person he impersonated.
几小时后，我神情恍惚地离开档案馆，重新进入了音像店，现在店里挤满了在苏联统治下长期无法获得这些商品和体验的顾客。他们似乎都对商店背后那座历史记忆之屋一无所知。充斥商店的俄罗斯流行乐那急促的节拍跟随着我穿过吱呀作响的大门，冲向街道，向着不远处的克里姆林宫飘去。

Some hours later, dazed, I left the archive and reentered the music store, now crowded with customers hungry for goods and experiences long unavailable under Soviet rule. They all appeared to be oblivious to the historical house of memories behind the shop. The insistent beat of Russian pop that filled the store followed me through the screeching door, burst onto the street, and billowed toward the Kremlin a short distance away.

一个关于斯大林时代的全新视角展现在我面前，尽管那年夏天我无法延长在莫斯科的停留时间，但在随后的几年里，我又多次回来访问。起初，我以为斯捷潘·波德卢布内的日记肯定是个例外。但在每次旅行中，我都发现了越来越多的日记，这些日记出自男女老少、穷人富人之手，也出自艺术家、知识分子、学生和家庭主妇之手。我在莫斯科及其周边的档案馆里发现了日记。其他的则来自私人渠道，由日记作者本人或其后代提供。其中几位日记作者邀请我去他们家讨论他们的生活记录。虽然藏有斯大林时代最大规模日记收藏的克格勃（KGB）档案馆依然对我关闭，但我得以阅读了一些日记的公开版本，以及该时期的许多其他出版的日记、信件和回忆录。

An entirely new perspective on Stalin’s time had opened up to me, and though I could not prolong my stay in Moscow that summer, I returned for further visits in the years that followed. In the beginning I believed that Stepan Podlubny’s diary had to be an exceptional case. But on each trip I found more and more diaries, written by men and women who were old and young, rich and poor, artists and intellectuals, students and housewives. I found diaries in archives in and around Moscow. Others came from private sources, offered by the diarists or their descendants. Several of these diarists invited me to their homes to discuss the records of their lives. While the KGB archives, which contain the single largest collection of Stalin-era diaries, remained closed to me, I was able to read published versions of some of those diaries, as well as many other published diaries, letters, and memoirs from the period.
有些日记一下午就能看完；有些则长达数千页。有些沉闷乏味；有些则充满了令人心碎又令人不寒而栗的告白。虽然有些日记作者从未审视过他们的内心世界，而那些让我越读越感兴趣的日记作者，往往会追问自己是谁，又该如何改变自己。这些内省和自我拷问的声音处于本书的核心，在书中我探讨了在一个宏大的“我们”时代，书写“我”这个词意味着什么。

Some diaries could be read in an afternoon; others were thousands of pages long. Some were dreary and bland; others brimmed with confessions both heartrending and chilling. And while some diarists never examined their inner worlds, the ones I found myself reading with mounting interest often asked themselves who they were and how they could change. These introspective and self-interrogating voices lie at the center of this book, where I explore what is meant by writing the word I in an age of a larger We.

许多学者利用社会和政治理论来解释极权政权如何运作。我则采取了不同的方法。在本书各页中出现的历史当事人使用着丰富且往往令人吃惊的语言进行书写：许多东西在字面上就显露出来，另一些则需要仔细体察。在重构这些日记作者的希望、困境和选择时，我一次又一次地发现，个人参与到革命时代之深，令人震惊。这些当事人并不代表整个苏联社会，但他们共用的自我语言有助于解释斯大林统治下的生活是什么样子的。他们的声音中回荡着乌托邦式的热情；他们向我们展示了一个既迷人又令人不安的时代，当时许多普通人都感到有一种冲动，要将自己的生活刻入革命和世界历史之中。

Many scholars have used social and political theories to explain how totalitarian regimes work. I have taken a different approach. The historical actors who parade across the pages of this book wrote in rich and often startling language: many revelations take place at the surface, but others call for careful attention. In reconstructing the hopes, dilemmas, and choices of these diarists, I found, time after time, an astounding depth of individual involvement in the revolutionary age. These actors do not speak for the whole of Soviet society, but the language of self that they share helps explain what life was like under Stalin’s rule. Their voices resonate with utopian fervor; they introduce us to a time at once fascinating and disturbing, when many ordinary people felt impelled to inscribe their lives into the revolution and into world history.
